utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Case number IT-01-47- T, the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Can we have the appearances for the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, assisted by Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this 177th day of our hearing, I wish to bid good morning to all those present; the Prosecution, the four lawyers present, the two accused, as well as all the persons within and without the courtroom. I would like that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber told the parties that this morning we will be rendering a decision in response to a motion for the clarification of points, and the decision has been finalised and will be recorded this morning. We have to render a decision on judicial notice of certain facts that were raised in two other cases. We are still waiting. I don't have the submissions of the Prosecution on this matter, and I hope it will not arrive too late. We are also waiting for the report of the expert who should be testifying on the 16th and 17th of February. We're also waiting for the submissions of the Prosecution. So that is as far as the outstanding motions requiring decisions stand. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our understanding was that we had until the 7th to file our response with respect to the judicial notice. We will be filing that certainly no later than Monday, if our understanding is correct in that respect. With respect to the expert report, once again, as we indicated earlier, we are awaiting not only the attachments to that report but also the additional material that the expert cites to, and we are simply unable to expedite that until we get that material from the Defence. Our view is that the attachments, since they are listed, they form part of the expert report and, in fact, the filing of that report is incomplete until such time as those attachments and any documents that he cites to are filed. We will again -- I assure everyone we will do our best, but we simply cannot be in a position to state our views until we have that expert report and its supporting materials and attachments in toto. While I'm on my feet, Mr. President, you will also recall on the 10th of January Mr. Bourgon indicated the Defence plans with respect to the military expert, hoping to call him commencing on the 28th of February. We have not seen any filing with respect to that expert report. Our understanding was it would have been filed by now. Perhaps our learned colleagues can give us a little bit of light on that. Again, we'll have a very difficult time complying with their plans in light of the Rule that will give us 30 days to consider that expert report on that issue. And again while I'm on my feet, Mr. Bourgon also raised the issue of a number of perhaps additional witnesses to be called by the Defence or -- and/or the use of Rule 92 bis statements. We did ask for at least copies of any statements the Defence currently have. As Your Honours and of course the Defence are aware, in order to get those 92 bis certificates and perhaps litigation on that, that could take a little bit of time, and we again ask if the Defence does in fact have written statements of any witnesses that they intend to seek 92 bis with respect to, we would ask for copies of those statements as quickly as possible so that we can at least begin formulating whether our position with respect to whether we need to cross-examine or would seek leave to have those witnesses brought in for cross-examination purposes. And I raise those issues because of course the Defence has indicated a proposed timetable for completing the Hadzihasanovic case, and it appears to us that that might not be possible due to these outstanding issues with respect to the expert reports and the 92 bis statements, and we simply raise that at this point for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to the Defence in a moment. There are several points raised. Regarding the witness that should come on the 16th and 17th of February, the Prosecution is waiting for the attachments. So there's a problem there. A second problem, which seems of capital importance to me, is the military expert and his report. Clearly it needs to be communicated quickly because you mentioned the 28th of February, and then there's the delay of 30 days and as it is normal to expect that this will be an important report, similar to General Reinhardt's one, so the Prosecution must be in a position to submit its position on those matters. As for this military expert, I should also like to know if -- is he a witness of both Defence teams or of one Defence team? Because the other Defence team is also entitled to have an expert report. Mr. Dixon is speaking, so I don't think he can hear what I'm saying. Mr. Dixon, I was saying that the military expert that is going to be called, will he be the witness of both Defence teams? Because you, too, are entitled to call your own expert witness. So what we would like to know is whether this witness is a joint, a common witness for both parties, or do you plan to have your own witness at some later point in time? Mr. Dixon, you can answer this question and then give the floor to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, the witness will be a joint military expert witness for both the accused. It was thought that it was most efficient in terms of saving time and being able to focus on essentially the same issues to have one expert to cover the position of both Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura. So the report will be a joint one filed, and in essence it will be the first joint witness within the case for Mr. Hadzihasanovic. So we are working with the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic to have the report finalised as soon as possible. But Ms. Residovic could give further details on that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking this for procedural reasons, because when you address your questions to the witness, the questions must not be leading. They must be absolutely neutral. That is why I'm asking, because if he were not your witness, you would be able, when your turn comes, to ask him quite leading questions. But as he's also your witness, I thought it necessary to refer to this. I give the floor now to the other Defence to respond to the points raised by Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we said last time, we did not receive the attachments from our expert regarding the organisation of the authorities. Three days ago, we did receive his attachments in the Bosnian language. They are being translated now, and possibly the translation will be completed by the end of the day. If not, they will be communicated to the Prosecution on Monday morning at the latest. They are tables, as can be seen, and certain overviews of the national structure and other structures in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the CV of the expert. As for other documents, as I said last time, in order to facilitate the work of the Prosecution, we will prepare a binder of documents which the Professor will be referring to in his expert report. However, in the report we have already disclosed the documents are indicated which had already been disclosed to the Prosecution, be they documents that have been admitted into evidence in this case or documents which are on the Defence list and which the Prosecution has in its possession. However, as I said, regardless of that fact, we will do our best to provide the Prosecution with a binder with a collection of all those exhibits and documents that the Professor refers to in his expert report. The simple reason why we haven't done that so far is that we don't have translations of all those documents. If the Prosecution wants us to provide this binder on Monday, but it would only include those that we have translations of. The others would be in the Bosnian-Herzegovinian version. That is what we can say so far. I wish to tell the Trial Chamber that in accordance with the Defence -- both Defence teams' planning, each of our teams has their own witnesses, especially fact witnesses. However, from the beginning we agreed that expert witnesses who discussed the historical context, the organisation of the authorities or military matters, would be proposed as joint witnesses, and that is what we have done. When we had the historian, as well as in the case of Professor Trnka, our colleagues from the Kubura Defence will treat those witnesses as being their own. So they will not be asking leading questions. As for our request for witnesses under 92 bis, our investigators in Sarajevo have taken statements from persons that will be proposed as 92 bis witnesses. That is, only statements would be filed. We currently have only one of those statements. We are expecting another two, possibly three, because one witness was on our list but for reasons of health he is unable to come, but his testimony would be repetitious. We have a problem with the taking of statements from international witnesses, and as we felt it would be better to file all the statements together, we will inform you on Monday whether we will apply this procedure or whether we would file a motion to accept these 92 bis statements from witnesses in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as others, that is, whether we would wait to collect all seven or eight statements under 92 bis, some of which need to be translated. That is as much as I'm able to say at this point in time. In view of the fact that the military expert is a joint witness and that we still haven't received his finding from him, together with Mr. Kubura's team we will address the matter during the weekend, and we will propose to the Trial Chamber a date for calling this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Both the Prosecution and the Defence will have time in the meantime to discuss these problems and to inform us should you encounter difficulties. I think we need to deal with a number of documents now. I shall give the floor now to the Prosecution, asking them whether they wish to tender any documents into evidence. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would tender the three documents that were shown to the witness yesterday, again with the same note that was used with respect to previous documents; that is, that they go only to refreshing recollection or credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those three documents which were the subject of extensive discussion, I turn to the Defence now. No objection? Fine. Mr. Registrar, three numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These three documents are admitted into evidence as Prosecution exhibits and in accordance with the conditions mentioned by the Prosecution just now, under the following numbers. The first document, with the ERN number 04034336, dated the 19th of September, 1993, admitted into evidence as Exhibit P947, and the English version P947/E. The second document, number ERN 04034329, dated the 24th of September, 1993, is admitted into evidence as Exhibit P948, and the English version P948/E. The third document, with the ERN number 04033837, dated the 22nd of November, 1993, is admitted into evidence as P949, with the English version P949/E. That ends the list, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 947, 948, 949 are admitted into evidence with the note that they were used to test the credibility or refresh the memory of the witness in accordance with our oral decision, so that there should be no ambiguity regarding these three documents. We now have a witness, and I will ask the usher to bring him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that you are hearing me in your own language. If that is the case, please tell me that you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, will you please tell me your first and last name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Hubo Hajrudin. I was born on the 4th of October 1964, in Visoko in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you employed today? Do you have a position? If so, which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am employed in the federal Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo. Currently I have the post of chief of the verification centre, a centre engaging in armaments control and international obligations linked to arms control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are an employee. Are you a military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By rank I am a brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I call you sir or general? Which do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigadier in our country is comparable with the rank of colonel, but you can address me whichever way you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, then. In 1992, 1993 - this is more than ten years ago - at the time, did you have a position or post? If so, which? If you were in the military, which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are referring to the beginning of the war or before the war, I can tell you both, but will you please tell me which you're inquiring about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I was an officer in the former JNA. I left it in the course of 1991. That is, I left the former Yugoslav People's Army at the beginning of 1992. As of the 6th of April I was engaged in the Territorial Defence of Zenica. So I was an officer in the intelligence organ, assistant commander for intelligence, and for a while in the staff I was chief of staff. When it was disbanded, I was reassigned to the command of the 3rd Corps, the organ for spatial structures. I was chief of that organ. It was part of the command of the 3rd Corps. After that, I was appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in an international or national court of law about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time, Your Honour, for me to be in any kind of court of law in the function of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence, which has planned an hour and a half of questions, but I draw their attention to the fact that we must necessarily complete our work by quarter to two, so make sure that we respect that schedule. You will have to answer questions put to you by the attorneys of one of the accused, that is General Hadzihasanovic. Once those questions are completed, it is possible that the attorneys for General Kubura may have questions for you as well. After that stage, the Prosecution, seated to your right, may also have questions for you within what we know as the cross-examination. And according to the procedure, they are entitled to ask you leading questions; that is, questions which may be suggestive and in favour of their case. However, in the examination-in-chief, the questions have to be neutral. Upon the completion of the cross-examination, the Defence may have additional questions for you linked to the previous questions. During this stage, it is quite possible for the parties to show you documents to elicit your comments. These will be military documents which they thought you may have seen or of which you may have some knowledge. That is why those documents may be shown to you. The three Judges who are in front of you may also ask you questions. According to the procedure, they can ask you anything they wish at any point in time, but we prefer to wait until the end to see whether we need to ask you anything to clarify what you have already said or to fill in any gaps that we may feel exist in the answers that you may have provided, and all of this in the interest of justice. Our procedure is an oral procedure, so we have no written report about what you are going to say, hence the importance of what you tell us. If you don't understand a question put to you, ask for a rephrasing. I wish to draw your attention to two points. First is that you have made the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, which excludes all false testimony. And the second point is that a witness may refuse to answer a question if he believes that this -- his reply may one day be used against him and to incriminate him, and the witness may say, "I do not wish to answer." This is an exceptional case which we have never come across. The Chamber may insist that the witness answer nevertheless but guaranteeing total immunity to the witness for any subsequent consequences, and this contributes to the whole truth being established. Should there be any problems, please let us know. We will be having two breaks for technical reasons until a quarter to two and also to give you a chance to take a rest, because you will see that answering questions can be quite tiring, hence the need to give you an opportunity to take a breather. It is now half past nine. We will have our first break at 10.30, that is in an hour, and then we will have another break around 12.30. So without further ado, I give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hubo. You've already said that you were an officer in the former JNA. Tell us, please, where you completed your military training, your military schools, and where you did your military service in the JNA before you left the JNA in 1991.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I completed the military secondary school, four years of that in Belgrade. After the military gymnasium in Belgrade, I continued studying at the Military Academy for two years. I completed those two years in Belgrade, one year in Rajlovac and one year in Zadar. Having completed the Military Academy I was deployed to the anti-aircraft defence missile section in Kragujevac, which is where I was until I left the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what rank did you have when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I left the JNA as lieutenant. That was my rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I'm going to use some documents with this witness, I should like to hand these documents to the witness straight away, and we have given copies to the Prosecution already. Also, while the documents are being distributed, there is one particular document which will be on our final list of exhibits, and that is document -- a document that was published in the BH Official Gazette. It is therefore an official document. And we have also disclosed it to the Prosecution, but it is in the B/C/S version. And as far as I understand, the Prosecution says that it does not mind us using the document in examining the witness. I now ask the Trial Chamber to allow us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, in response to the President of the Trial Chamber, you said that you worked in the District Staff of the Territorial Defence at the beginning as an officer in the intelligence service and later on as a representative of the chief of staff when it was disbanded. Can you remember when the District Staff was, in fact, disbanded, of the Territorial Defence, I mean, of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: I can't give you an exact date here and now because it was a process, and you know that when units are formed or disbanded this requires a certain amount of time. But it was, generally speaking, the period between, as far as I can recall, October 1992 up until April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you, Mr. Hubo, to take a look at a document which comes after number 1. It is P320. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a document informing the municipal Territorial Defence Staff that the District Staff will cease to exist, and you worked on that staff.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This document is dated the 16th of April, 1993. It is an order, and then it says "Information to the command of the 3rd Corps," stating that on the basis of the information received, the Zenica District Staff was being abolished. This is the standard type of document that was sent round. It was a final act, and the preparations to bring in this final act had already been conducted. So it is a document that is of an official nature, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, Mr. Hubo, that after the abolishment of the District Staff of the Territorial Defence, you took up another duty and you went to the command of the 3rd Corps as head of spatial structures there. Can you tell us, please, what that organ did. What was its function?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said that it was a process for the formation of a corps with all the units. So the corps command was being established, and the municipal staffs of Territorial Defence and the units that the individual defence staffs had had still not been abolished completely. So this organ, as it was called, was within the 3rd Corps Command staff, and its duty was as follows: It was in charge of coordinating individual activities that the municipal staffs used to do in this transitional phase until their final abolishment. So the abolition, the disbanding did not stop when the District Staff were disbanded, but this function was taken over by the 3rd Corps in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, would you now take a look at the next document, that is to say document number 2, and the number at the top is 1381.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: That is a document from the 3rd Corps Command which I compiled. I can see my initials there. And it concerns the following: It is an explanation to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence, and it says to the attention of the Operative Group, which means that at that time, the operative groups were being formed, and it says: "In connection with your dilemma about the manner of reporting, such-and-such a date, we hereby inform you that there are no changes in your duty of reporting to the organ for territorial based units of the 3rd Corps Command which took over the authority of the OPSO when the Zenica OKSO was dissolved. You are therefore obliged to send weekly intelligence reports according to the methodology which was submitted to you." So this therefore proves or confirms that although in the month of August, what I said a moment ago, that the Municipal Staff still remained but their competencies were taken over by the 3rd Corps Command. So that is a standard document and response that we sent out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you said that the process of abolishing the municipal defence staffs was under way and they were still in existence during that period of time. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, up until what time did these staffs exist? How long were they in existence on the territory of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you a date with any certainty, but I can tell you that throughout 1993 they still existed. On a case-by-case basis, they were transformed more rapidly in some areas and in others this process was slower. Once again depending on the front line, the reinforcement by troops and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you worked in affairs linked to the municipal defence staffs, take a look at our next document, which is number 3, and the number of that document is DH1501. You will find that number at the top of the document. And tell us, please, what kind of document this is. Are you familiar with the document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Madam, this is a document, one of many, in fact, which are of similar content which the command -- 3rd Corps Command wrote, as it says here, on the 20th of October, 1993 - that's the date of this particular document - and it has to do with organisational changes in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, if I can put it that way. So this is a proposal which was sent out to the staff of the Supreme Command of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Hubo, is this document the proposal for organisational changes or the establishment and restructuring of certain units? Is this -- are these authorisations and competencies of the commander of some military unit, in fact, vis-a-vis his superior command? That is to say, to table proposals and to send them out to that command.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Of course this is in keeping with the authorisations of the corps command, and this is standard practice. It is quite usual procedure when it comes to restructuring any unit, establishing a unit, abolishing a unit, or anything of that kind. It is of the units of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the corps commander, in order to compile a proposal of this kind with respect to the establishment of a unit, must he have special authorisation to do so or does this duty come from the very functions inherent in the commander?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow your question. Could you make that question clearer, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The function and duties of a commander pursuant to the law and status of a commander as such, does it include the authority vested in the officer to make proposals to the command with respect to organisational matters? That is to say, can he propose the establishment or restructuring of anybody or the abolishment of anybody in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The commander does have this right. He has every right to propose things of this kind, and final authorisation is given by the staff of the Supreme Command. But the commander does have the right to -- and duty, if I may say so, to propose things along this line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the second part of my question, which I don't suppose you understood very well and thank you for bringing that to my attention, I'll make it clearer: In addition to the rules, did the commander have to have any special authorisations or was he able to do -- proceed in this manner, the way he did in this case?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said this was standard practice, so he doesn't have to have any special authorisation because the -- a commander's competencies include his right to make proposals of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you took up your duties in the 3rd Corps, did you in the staff of the 3rd Corps engage in any other duties in addition to carrying about and coordinating the work of the municipal defence staffs, for example?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: As I have said, we were in the composition of the staff, and in view of the number of members we had or, rather, we had very few people, to make myself clearer, so there was a few people and their capabilities were modest, I had to work as the operative officer because it was the operative organ within the corps staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, at one point did you take up some other duties; and, if so, tell us which and when.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: At one point in time, that is to say after approximately -- or, rather, when I had completed this business around the municipal staffs and their establishment and their functioning, I was assigned in the second half of 1993 as assistant commander for organisational and mobilisational Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. matters and personnel matters. That was an organ of the corps command which was within the composition of the command, and the assistant commander was directly under the commander of the corps himself, the corps commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Hubo, what kind of work the organ for organisational, mobilisational and personnel matters did, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The duties I had at the time, or, rather, this body, if I can put it that way, because as I say there were few people in it, so this organ too suffered from a lack of personnel. But anyway, its duties were the following: To form the unit, to re-establish or restructure the units, to disband the units, and the organisational orders for the structure of the command to see that there was a full complement of men and materiel, to resolve the status of individuals, see to status matters and other affairs which any staff has to deal with, and these are all difficult matters to resolve and require a great deal of time and attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, tell me, please, what rules and regulations governed the functioning of your organ and its competencies and you yourself?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: What I did at the beginning in this newly established situation was the following: The law on defence, that was the main document or, rather, its provision on the criteria and normative acts for the deployment of citizens and materiel in the armed forces and other needs of defence. This was published in the Official Gazette 1922 [as interpreted] of the then Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then my other framework or, rather, our framework under which we functioned was orders by the Supreme Command issued by way of instructions and so on. So those are the documents. The degree on criteria and normatives, that was an internal document and so were the others, and they were documents that we had taken over from the former JNA; that is to say, documents that had not been published until then but were taken over, rules on the mobilisation of the armed forces which we had been using hitherto.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at our next document now, number 10. It is the document in the B/C/S version. Would you read the preamble and the title of the document and tell me whether that is the document that you referred to just now. Was that the document you meant?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, this is a decree having the force of law on the criteria and normative dispositions on the disposition of citizens and resources in the armed forces and other needs of defence. So this was our basic document. It was on the basis of this document that we were able to function.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 20, line 21, there has been a mistake of when the document was published. The witness said in the Official Gazette 19/92, and the date is 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says 1922. So that is a slip. I don't assume you would use 1922 as your basic document.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I apologise, but that is the document that we used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you worked in the area of mobilisation for people and materiel, I should like to ask you now to explain to Their Honours, to the Trial Chamber, the manner in which, pursuant to this decree, you undertook mobilisation of individuals into the BH army. How were they recruited?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It was the duty of the commands at the level of brigades and independent units was the following: On the basis of the order and regulations prescribed, to propose the troops necessary for the individual units. And this plan for the mobilisation of men and materiel contained the number of soldiers required, and these were distributed into what we call the VES, the military speciality of each individual according to their files and as registered with the national defence secretary. So these were the replenishment plans. And so this proposal for the replenishment plans was sent on to the Secretariats for National Defence. And the competent Secretariats for National Defence, having reviewed the situation and the -- how far the units were replenished, how many troops it needed, and looking at the available men outside the armed forces given a time of imminent war and should war break out, they would approve a final replenishment plan, and then they would send this plan to the individual departments of defence, and they were duty-bound and had the authority to act upon that plan and call up the military conscripts and send them to a particular military unit. So that was the procedure. It was common practice, and it was a very clear-cut practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, on several occasions in answering my questions earlier on, you said the competent organ of the Ministry of Defence, and then you said that once the plan had been approved through its own line, it would send it to the different departments and units. Tell me, please, the Ministry of Defence itself and its competent organs or, rather, its departments to which the replenishment plan was sent down, were they organs within the composition of the BH army, and did the -- was the army superior to those organs, the organs which approved the replenishment plans?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The BH army had a civilian commander, that is to say the president of the -- Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina had its government, within the frameworks of the government the Ministry of Defence functioned just like every other ministry, if I can say so, given the conditions that prevailed. So the army was not superior to the ministry nor what -- did it ever assume that role. It was -- or, rather, the Ministry of Defence and its sections in the field in the different territories as they were organised as civilian authority in the districts and municipalities, they were in charge and they performed the functions of mobilisation. So the army had a secondary role there, just like any army, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you said that every military unit, that is to say a brigade and so on, independent unit, was duty-bound to propose a replenishment plan for the master plan. Tell me, how was this plan compiled?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I've already said, I think, in response to one of your questions that this was done exclusively on the basis of the different formations that were set up. You had corps right up to independent battalions. So on the basis of the individual units. In war, for materiel resources, no formation or establishment was prescribed, but it was for manpower. So this was done on the basis of establishment documents, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now, please: Who determined the establishment books or documents for individual military units? And the wartime composition of that unit, was it identical to what it was in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: All the formations or units and all the documents and books that existed, and there were different types depending on the different types of units, was prescribed and organised by the Ministry of Defence. And I think that during one period in the war the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact, issued authorisation to the staff of the Supreme Command for it to be able to authorise the establishments themselves as a -- working as a Ministry of Defence organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you something else. Perhaps you've already answered it, but the establishment, providing for a certain number of men per unit, is there a difference during wartime and peacetime? Would the structure, number of the men be different in a unit in wartime than it would in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The only difference was that in wartime conditions, it was prescribed that the replenishment of men should be 110 per cent compared to the planned formation, so there would be a leeway of 10 per cent. That is to say they would plan 10 per cent more men because of the casualties during the war and during the battles and so on. So 110 per cent in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the previous questions, you said that once the plan had been approved for the replenishment of troops, that then the departments of Defence would send out -- would call up the individuals, the men, the troops themselves. Could you tell me, Mr. Hubo, what a military unit did if the recruit did not -- or conscript did not respond to the call-up by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I've already said that the Ministry of Defence or defence departments had the job of calling up conscripts and to send them to the units. So right up until the time that a conscript has not reported to the unit, it was the Ministry of Defence that was in charge. The law prescribed what subsequent measures were to be taken by the competent authorities should conscripts fail to turn up, fail to report to the authorities to take up their duties within a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, tell me, please, in wartime was there another way of going about securing a full complement of soldiers for military units and not only by the call-up on the part of the civilian defence organ? And if there was another way, another way of doing this, did a military unit have any obligations in that regard after men were recruited into the unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: You mean did a military unit have the possibility of engaging men themselves? Pursuant to the law, the military unit the area of combat, if the competent organ under the minister of defence was not able to mobilise troops, in extraordinary circumstances it was able to engage a certain -- with conscripts themselves. But it -- the military unit had the duty in the shortest space of time of tallying the numbers in the unit with the Ministry of Defence. That means that the Ministry of Defence, once again, had to have a complete list of men and place its stamp on the document authorising the number of men recruited.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In wartime, in addition to the military conscripts, were you able to take in individuals who were not military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In wartime in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had volunteers as well. And pursuant to the law, all military conscripts -- these were men from the ages of 16 to 65, I believe. Now, the other categories, other age groups were not -- did not have to comply. But we did have some women, for example. In fact, we had 5.000 women fighters as volunteers at one point in time. Of course, nobody turned them back. It was their right to defend their country. So we took them in. And then we had some people who were over the age of 65 who came to us to join up. And then we had other categories of people, that is to say people who were not nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. They were usually people from the former Yugoslavia, from ex-Yugoslavia who happened to find themselves in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They could also join up. And some of them came to us and joined up in the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a military unit took in volunteers of this kind, did it have any duties vis-a-vis the defence ministry or was it its exclusive prerogative?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Once again the procedure would be clear cut. The unit, if it did take people in of this kind, volunteers or whatever, they would have to have these people registered with the defence ministry. They would have to have a list of persons and send the list to the Ministry of Defence with these individual categories and special or separate files would be opened up for these people, people who had joined the unit in some other fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues have been -- have told me that on page 25, line 15, it has not been recorded that the witness said that the military unit could mobilise men if the organ of the Ministry of Defence was not capable of doing so. So since the witness said this, I can repeat the question. Or can you just make a note for the record of what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't hear the interpretation in my own language, and I have the headphones on. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, Mr. Hubo, what was the policy of the 3rd Corps, which you joined after the district headquarters and staff was disbanded? Tell me, what was the policy of the 3rd Corps with respect to mobilisation? What did the commander and his command request from military units to fill in their units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Our policy stemmed from the law, the orders of the Supreme Command Staff, and in the first place we requested that the units and subordinate commands should carry out their obligations accordingly, which meant abiding by the decree, abiding by the decree, abiding by orders and the structure that had been laid down for each unit. So the policy was that everyone do his job properly. The competence for mobilisation was with the hands of the defence ministry, and we requested that it should be so. The organisation and structuring of units was within the competence of the army, and we requested that it should be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hubo, regardless of this very clear-cut policy of the 3rd Corps Command, what kind of problems did the army encounter when it came to mobilisation from the beginning of the war until the end of 1993? If you can tell us briefly what those problems were.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It is difficult to list all those problems briefly, because mobilisation is both a political and economic and social issue. It entails a number of measures and procedures in order to mobilise people for defence. However, in that period of time when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as a state, a certain number of people left with the former JNA. They were military conscripts too. Then all the civilian bodies had still not been constituted. Then there was a high influx of refugees. There were areas of wartime operations. Then there was the lack of functioning of other segments of society, hesitation among people about various matters. Then rather a confusing system. In other words, the system was slowly breaking down. And under those conditions, it was very hard to carry out the mobilisation as would have been done in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Evidence has been shown in court already that already in June 1992, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed a state of war and general mobilisation. Tell me, what were the reasons for the proclamation of a state of war and general mobilisation that this did not result in the mobilisation of each and every conscript? Or in other words, how did all this evolve according to your personal experience with respect to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: When talking about defence, this is a complex issue implying the commitment of all entities in society. In the process of defence, if we focus on combat - that is defence in the narrow sense of the word, combat on the front - does not mean that only soldiers take part. There's the economy of a country, the general life. A certain number of conscripts are engaged within a certain age group, and they are assigned to army units. A certain number of conscripts are assigned to the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. A number of conscripts are assigned to the judiciary, another number to the educational system, to the economy, to the hospitals and so on. So in all areas of life, according to the law they are all conscripts but life has to continue. And if the war had lasted five days, all could be called up and after that go back to their jobs, but that was not the case. So the law regulates the wartime assignment of each and every conscript, which includes engagement in the army, in the MUP, and at workplaces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, a moment ago you said that the system fell apart. Did this have any kind of impact on the ability to mobilise people? Did the competent bodies have records of military conscripts, files? If not, where were they, and what kind of problems did you encounter in that area in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said that this was a highly complex issue, the issue of mobilisation, and it is very difficult to explain even if I were to take hours. But there were many difficulties that stood in the way of efficient mobilisation. Certain legal and legitimate departments of defence were abolished in certain municipalities. What does that mean? It means that certain segments of the SDS took with them files. Then we had thefts of certain files. And every military conscript had his own file in the Ministry of Defence containing all data about him, his speciality, and everything else. Those files were lacking. Then in all the municipalities, these bodies had not been constituted. Then we had refugees coming. People were no longer in their own communes, nor had they been registered in the ones they had come to. So we had many difficulties which hindered the normal smooth running of the mobilisation process. I don't know if I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The district defence staff that you were working in in 1992 and the beginning of 1993 and later in the 3rd Corps up until the end of 1993, did they have the materiel requirements to be able to mobilise and admit all people according to formation? Did you have the necessary weapons and other necessary equipment to be able to mobilise all the recruits?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said that the former Yugoslavia had detailed mobilisation plans. However, the newly developed situation was such that the former Yugoslav People's Army withdrew more or less all the weapons of the Territorial Defence with it so that the Territorial Defence was left without most weapons. So it was not possible nor necessary to mobilise everyone, which means that we mobilised according to the possibilities we had; that is, if we could match the weapons with the recruits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, were you aware that because of the impossibility to carry out the mobilisations, some of which you have described, were you confronted with the occurrences when people self-organised themselves or acted individually in small groups totally outside the command and control of organised legitimate authorities, or were there no such problems in the area of the 3rd Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Slovenia, later in Croatia, and of course in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are people of different ethnicities, and there were links with all those newly formed countries. A certain number of people realised that a threat was imminent, and a certain number of people self-organised themselves on some territorial or political bases for defence. And these were groups, groups of men who were not accountable to anyone. They just defended their local communities, their villages, and so on. They were just there. And they probably had a certain number of light weapons, hunting weapons, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the situation with weapons that you have referred to, in the process of mobilisation were weapons taken from people? Were they confiscated, or did those weapons remain private property, those that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: If you're referring to weapons that individuals may have purchased or acquired in various ways, those weapons, with the subsequent formation of the army, those weapons became part of state property. But as for personal weapons, a person who purchased a rifle or a pistol, he wouldn't give it to anyone else, if we're talking about the initial stages, the beginnings of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As those personal weapons, as you say, were the source of the arming of the army, tell me, how many people in 1992 and 1993, how many were -- had to rely on that single weapon that was mobilised with an individual?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, this depended, but sometimes there would be up to five men to one rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, I would now like to ask you about the mobilisation of the 3rd Corps, which was carried out in accordance with the orders and the criteria you mentioned. Was that mobilisation something that was carried out in one go or did it take place over a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Mobilisation is a process that many people do not understand, especially those who were not involved in it. I have to underline once again that over a certain period of time, you had various cases. So mobilisation was a process that went on from the beginning until the end of the war. Some people who joined from the beginning were mobilised and then demobilised. But then there were cases when one individual may have been mobilised four or five times and demobilised or, rather, assigned to other posts, such as doctors and engineers. So they would be assigned to positions where they were most needed in the assessment of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the concrete tasks you had when you took charge of the body for organisational matters. As we were talking about this process, what was the situation that you found in the 3rd Corps organ when you joined it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: When I took up this duty, I found there a man, and there should have been many more. But this was quite understandable, because there was a high degree of fluctuation of personnel. We had units that were not up to strength. They were about 70 per cent complete, which was not sufficient for a unit to be properly established. We had a large influx of people and ineffective cooperation with the civilian authorities. Records were not very complete, and so on. The situation was quite chaotic, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you joined this body, was the 3rd Corps Commander, to the best of your knowledge, satisfied with the mobilisation and its results?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The commander would be the one to answer that question best. Clearly the commander did take steps, at least as far as I know, to improve the situation or to put things in order in the way I've already described. Among other things, my predecessor -- now why he was replaced, I assume it was precisely because the commander was not satisfied. He wanted more. Though I find it rather embarrassing to say that for my predecessor, but this was quite customary, to replace people with those who were better qualified in the assessment of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at document under tab 6, please. P192. So it's an exhibit in this case. And it is a report of the 3rd Corps Commander. And will you please look now at a page with the ERN number 1851606. Have you found the page? At the top the page number is 01851606.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please read out this text for me to be able to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it would be better to indicate the number of the page in the English version, because 01 et cetera, is the B/C/S. So please give us the page number for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just before the sub-heading "Combat morale."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's page 15. Page 15 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So would you please read out, which is very brief in the Bosnian. These are paragraphs that also appear in English. Have you read it? Mr. Hubo, can you tell me whether this is a concise description of the problems you referred to and which the commander is highlighting in his -- in this report?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This reflects the actual state of affairs with regard to these points, and each sentence here implies taking a large number of measures for dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning when speaking of the responsibilities of the body that you headed, and you said that it assigned and reassigned people, tell me, did you have in the records of your organ which units existed in the corps structure? Or, rather, could you tell me which were the data that you had available to you in your organ.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: When I arrived, I didn't find my predecessor there, but I found some documents, and one of the most important for me was the report of combat units regarding their strength. And these are referred to, that is, to what extent each unit was fully replenished, and this was very important for our organ to plan our activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For this very reason, I would like to ask you to look at the previous two pages before the part I asked you to read out. In English, those would be pages 14 and 15 -- and 13, I'm sorry. And 13. And in our language, page numbers 0185603 and 604 and 605. Will you please tell me, on page 603, would you begin with where it says, "The 3rd Corps is composed of five operative groups," and look at those operation groups, units, and other bodies, and tell me whether this report reflects the state of affairs with respect to the units that had been established in the 3rd Corps that you were aware of as an operative and later as the head of this department.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps consists of five operations groups and they are listed here: Four independent brigades, which are again listed; three independent battalions, and these are listed; a light artillery and rocket battalion; a logistics base; an electronic reconnaissance and counter-electronic operations company; and a training centre. Also within the 3rd Corps 15 municipal defence staffs had been formed. These are listed, with 23 anti-sabotage detachments and eight independent companies. This, for me, was the organic composition of the command and units of the 3rd Corps, which we further developed. I can also say that it is quite clear that many units and -- existed which made it difficult to operate with such a large number of units, and the problem of control and command was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the next page. They're referring to manpower levels. You've said it was very important to have these figures. These figures that you see here, did they reflect the manpower levels in units when you took over your position in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This was the situation I found at the time. The situation, as it is described here, is based on reports received from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, on the title page of this document, you see that the commander drafted this report in August 1993. It is a report prepared for a meeting held in Zenica with the commander of the army. Tell me, would the corps commander in his report list all the units that he has as part of the organic structure, that is all the units that he knows are within his organic composition, whether they're linked to operations groups or independent units and battalions? Is it customary for a commander presenting a review of his corps to include all data about all units existing within his corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: This report was not compiled exclusively by the commander but the whole command respecting all elements, and I see no reason why anything should be left out. In fact, it is compulsory to include everything, obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of the organisational structure of the 3rd Corps, could there be an independent detachment linked to the 3rd Corps which the commander would not mention in this report?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: That would not be normal. It would have to be mentioned either here or in the Ministry of Defence. It would have to exist somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Hubo, since you said that there were problems with respect to recruits failing to respond to the call-up, but it became your problem only if -- when they failed to join. Then you also mentioned the problem of the fluctuation of manpower. What were the measures taken by the 3rd Corps Command against those abandoning units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: The prescribed measures were as follows: After a certain period of time, we would verify why soldiers did not turn up. If some had legitimate reasons to be absent, then these would be registered. I must say these were not soldiers who were living in barracks. They would be at some 20 kilometres distance from headquarters, because from front lines they would go home. And if it was not possible to establish a reason, then requests to bring him in would be issued to the military police battalion. And after searching for him, he would -- the police would have to take him in. And if they failed to find those conscripts, then measures were taken, as envisaged by law, to scratch them from the record. So after all disciplinary measures were exhausted, they were scratched.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was according to the law, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to adjourn now, and we will resume at five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the floor. Of course once the accused are seated. They are arriving now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, just before the break, you were speaking about the law and regulations and what they stipulated with respect to the military unit should anybody -- any of the soldiers decide to leave the unit of their own accord. Tell me, please, as a member of the command of the 3rd Corps, do you happen to know whether these measures of going out to look for these people and bringing -- taking them into custody, whether the 3rd Corps did engage in this process when anybody decided to leave of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This was done as far as they were able to. I remember during a period of time later on when we were establishing the units, we did have a review of how many people had left and what was done about it, and as far as I remember, there were about 3.000 requests for searches to be conducted to find the people. The military police battalion was given a list of about 3.000, which means that there were a lot of them and reflects the very difficult situation that prevailed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the process of mobilisation and replenishment of units had many problems to contend with, but I'm asking you this now,

utterances.speaker: MR. HUBO
utterances.text: If the commander, Commander Hadzihasanovic was corps commander from November 1992 to the 1st of November 1993, was that the period of time -- was it sufficient time to establish an army, to the best of your knowledge, in view of the fact that you're engaged in matters of that kind?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, the process of establishing an army lasts far longer in peacetime under normal conditions. It's a lengthy process. So if there was no war going on and you had the proper system functioning, a minimum of six months would be required to establish a corps or command. The former JNA established the Kragujevac Corps, for example over a long period of time. So this process of establishment for the BH army and the corps lasted, as far as I know, to the end of the war. And even to the present day, we are still in the process of restructuring and establishing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the federation. So my answer to you is this: Taking into account those strict dates, you could not have done that. It is a lengthy process, an ongoing one, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back, Mr. Hubo, to the portion of the report -- in fact, what you read out to the Trial Chamber, the units which in August 1993 were within the composition of the 3rd Corps. You read this out to us. We have it in writing. But now a leading question: The Mujahedin was not among those units, was it? I don't think you mentioned Mujahedin. So let me ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to ask that type of leading question, Mr. President, with the Court's permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since was already asked, has already been asked, he can answer it. Strictly speaking, you are not supposed to ask questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, I did ask a leading question. Anyway, in this text reviewing the units, did you see mention of the Mujahedin detachment anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: On this piece of paper there is no mention of the El Mujahedin attachment and many other units which were formed later on, at a subsequent stage, a much later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, can you tell me whether any other state organs of the superior command insisted upon the fact that the policy of mobilisation and establishment of units be conducted in conformity and pursuant to the law?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Of course. We had, if I can say so, different lines of functioning. One was the army chain. That is to say the staff of the Supreme Command through its corps and subordinate units, that was one chain of control and command. The other chain or line down was the BH Ministry of Defence at the top. Then the district Secretariats for National Defence, right down to the lower defence levels. So we did recognise and we asked for strict recognition of these chains and the duties incumbent upon each of the links in the chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look document number 8. 1407 is its number. This is a document of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take a look at point 1, line -- lines 1, 2, and 3. Do they reflect the policy of the Supreme Command which you endeavoured, as you said a moment ago, to put into practice as far as was possible?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I see here that the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 21st of August, 1993, wrote an order. I've never seen this order before. However, it does reflect the situation and the need for the undertaking of measures to ensure the unimpeded mobilisation of conscripts in the manner and according to the procedure which was prescribed. And this order, I assume, refers to the civilian organs of authority because, as I've already stated, we had a different situation there. There was a lack of organisation. We didn't find our way very well. So each of the individual instances were asked to do their job as best as they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you arrived to head this organ of the 3rd Corps in the autumn of 1993, did you, viewing the problems in hand, undertake measures to cooperate with the civilian organs, especially the Ministry of Defence, in order to and in the interests of both the army and the defence of the country, to coordinate and dovetail and promote that procedure?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: We had a clear-cut stand on that score. Our level of command in the corps and with the respect to the civilian corps was the district secretariats, and in exceptional cases municipal secretariats. We had situations in which we had, for example, the Banja Luka district with the conscripts from Banja Luka. We had established that on the territory of the 3rd Corps. Then we had another district, the Travnik district, at one point. The Zenica district was another, and the Sarajevo district. So that was that. Now, our additional efforts went along the arms -- along the lines of contacting and coordinating all these instances, which is what we did. The whole time we helped them in terms of personnel, in terms of technical resources and tried to comply with what they asked for to enable them to function in -- in accordance with the law and the provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago when I asked the leading question I did, I mentioned the El Mujahedin detachment. I'm asking you this now: When you took up duties in this organ, did you encounter any El Mujahedin -- any documents for an El Mujahedin detachment saying that it was within the composition of the 3rd Corps at all?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: No. I never came across the necessary documentation for that, neither was that unit mentioned in any of the reports or any document whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the following document now, please. It is number 9, and it is an order on the establishment of the El Mujahedin detachment. The number of the document is P439. And in view of what you were telling us earlier on about the detachment's formation or any other military unit, that this presupposes formation from the staff of the Supreme Command, would you take a look at the first paragraph in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps to form an El Mujahedin detachment pursuant to a proposal of the formations that you are duty-bound to send in to the staff for authorisation. Did you ever, in keeping with the law or practice on the ground, make proposals for establishments that were supposed to be sent up to the superior command for approval?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I've already said that the corps command did not establish formations. It did not establish formations. So this portion of the order, this paragraph, is in fact an order which was a little different from the usual type of order. I can explain this to you or comment, but this was out of the ordinary. It wasn't the corps command who was duty-bound to send in a formation to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you took up your duties in the area of mobilisation, did you find a book of formations or establishments in place when you arrived according to which each of the units was to be formed in -- established, including this detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: Well, I did come across some of the formation or establishment books and documents, if I can call them that, which did apply to various units, detachments, brigades, and so on, but I'm not quite clear on what you mean. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This book of formation -- for the formation of the Mujahedin detachment, did you come across that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: No. No. The orders usually said the high command, Supreme Command orders you to establish, according to the establishment book, et cetera, et cetera. In this case there was none of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find an order from the commander as to what this detachment was supposed to look like, an order for the formation of such a detachment handed down to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: It was the duty of the command corps, once they received an order to that effect, in this case from the Supreme Command staff, that the corps command should write its own order, issue its own order, which de facto was the order to be implemented, and that order contains far more details and elements relating to the establishment or abolishment of any unit. As far as I know, I never saw an order of that kind, neither did I come across it when I took up my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you find an information about the establishment of that order, that detachment, with a list of its command, the seat or headquarters of the power -- command, the method of replenishment and other important elements which would testify to the fact that that detachment was actually in existence within the structure of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what did that mean to you in practical terms? Practically speaking, what did that mean? Did the Mujahedin detachment in 1993 exist then? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: In this specific case it was not in existence. It did not exist. And as far as I was concerned, that detachment did not exist pursuant to all the elements and documentation available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, since you said that you stayed on performing these -- this same function, these same duties later on, tell me this: In 1993, did you know, were you aware of how many foreigners or Bosnian nationals there were in that detachment, if it had existed, either foreign national or Bosnian nationals?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: I said that I had no idea about the existence of the detachment at all, so I can't tell you how many men there were in it, whether they were Bosnian nationals or foreign nationals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Hubo, tell me this: At any time during your further work in the 3rd Corps, was there any establishment of this El Mujahedin unit; and if so, tell us when that might have come into being and what you know about that in general terms. What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: At a set stage when the corps was being established, that is to say 1994 and 1995 principally, I cannot tell you exactly what period of time, but there were contacts of this type. That is to say, somebody came in as a representative and said they had been sent, et cetera. This was an attempt, therefore, as I say, at some kind of establishment or to receive documents as to the number and so on. I have to stress that for a unit to be established, you must know in advance what you wish to have; how many men, how many men you have available. There are a lot of elements. Now, later on in the subsequent phase, there were some contacts in the sense of providing some sort of -- some lists, lists of some kind which were not valid lists or exact lists or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hubo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I should like to thank the Defence team. Mr. Dixon has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Only the one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown Prosecution Exhibit 192 which contained within it a list of the various units within the 3rd Corps and their manpower levels. Can you please confirm that the procedure that you described for the way in which units within the Bosnian army are replenished applied in the same way to each of the brigades and units mentioned in that document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the procedure was the same for all units. That means that after an order was received by the corps command, or from the corps command, a proposal for the replenishment plan was drafted, which was then sent out for authorisation to the competent Secretariats of Defence, and once they had authorised these, adopted these as a final plan for replenishment, the plan was sent down to the municipalities, and they then called up the men and sent the conscripts to a particular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I'm going to give the floor now to the Prosecution for the cross-examination. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we commence the cross-examination, I would respectfully ask that the witness be escorted out of the courtroom for a few moments so that I can address the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We informed the Defence earlier this week, Mr. President, about another new document that we might be wanting to show either this witness or the witness who testified yesterday. This is a document that appears to be authored by the current witness. The document is dated 7 May 1995. However, on the face of the document, it purports to have information about the presence of foreigners in the 3rd Corps as early as the summer of 1992. In light of the witness's answers -- the document also on its face refers to the El Mujahedin. In light of the witness's answers, this document certainly, in our opinion, would be one which could go to the witness's credibility. I raise this issue now so as to hopefully expedite proceedings in the event I'm allowed to do this. This document, Mr. President, came from the Bosnian intelligence and security agency, which is the new name of one of the agencies in Bosnia. It's known as OSA.
